title: Debugging and profiling
jupyter: python3
---

A model can go wrong in three ways: it stops with an error, it runs but gives an answer that looks wrong, or it runs too slowly. This page goes through the tools Starsim has for each, in roughly the order to reach for them. Most of them work on the measles model from the [tutorials](../tutorials/t1_intro.qmd): an SIR with β = 1.9 per day and an infectious period of 8 days, so R0 = 1.9 × 8 ≈ 15.

```{python}
import starsim as ss
ss.options(jupyter=True)

S, I, R = ss.states('S I R')
infection = S >> I @ 1.9*I        # β = 1.9 per day
recovery  = I >> R @ ss.days(8)   # Infectious for 8 days on average
measles = ss.Disease(infection, recovery, init_prev=0.001)
sim = ss.Sim(measles, total_pop=100_000, stop=ss.days(50))
sim.run()
```

For mistakes that are known to catch people out, see [Common pitfalls](troubleshooting_pitfalls.qmd); to ask for help with a problem, see [A minimal reproducible example](troubleshooting_mre.qmd).

## Reading an error

When Starsim can't build or run a model, it raises an error that names what is wrong in the terms of the model, and says what to do about it. Here the parameter β is misspelled:

```{python}
try:
    ss.Sim(measles, pars=dict(betta=2.0), total_pop=100_000, stop=ss.days(50)).run()
except ss.errors.UnknownParameter as error:
    print(error)
```

Each kind of error has a name, here `UnknownParameter`, so it can be looked up (`help(ss.errors.UnknownParameter)` says when it is raised) and caught by name, as above. All of them are listed in `ss.errors`. Most mistakes are caught when the sim is built (`sim.init()`, which `sim.run()` calls first), before any time step is taken, so an error usually comes at once rather than after a long run.

## Reading what a run prints

A run prints what it is running and how, the R0 of each disease, any notes, and a closing line with the size and timing of the peak. Read these first: most surprises are explained there. A note is something Starsim assumed or noticed that is worth knowing, and doesn't stop the run. For example, in an SEIR model, `init_prev` puts people in E, where a new infection starts, so nobody is infectious at first:

```{python}
S, E, I, R = ss.states('S E I R')
infection = S >> E @ 1.9*I
latency   = E >> I @ ss.days(10)
recovery  = I >> R @ ss.days(8)
seir = ss.Disease(infection, latency, recovery, init_prev=0.001, name='measles')
seir_sim = ss.Sim(seir, total_pop=100_000, stop=ss.days(100))
seir_sim.run()
```

The notes are kept in `sim.notes`, even when nothing is printed (`verbose=0`):

```{python}
seir_sim.notes
```

Some messages are warnings rather than notes: the run continues, but something probably needs attention (for example, a fitted parameter that ended at one of its bounds). To stop at the first warning instead, so that a script can't carry on past one unnoticed, turn warnings into errors:

```python
ss.options(warnings='error')
```

## Checking the model as built

Starsim fills in whatever a model leaves out: the population size, the distribution of each duration, how people mix, the unit of time, and which solver to use. `describe()` lists the whole model as it was built, with each value that Starsim chose itself marked as guessed. If a result looks wrong, check here that the model is the one you meant:

```{python}
sim.describe()
```

`equations()` gives the same model as the equations of an ODE, which is often the quickest way to check that each rate is what you meant (for example, that a transmission is frequency-dependent, β S I / N, and not density-dependent, β S I):

```{python}
measles.equations()
```

When two sims that should agree don't, `ss.diff()` compares them in their own terms: their states and transitions, their parameters, their settings (such as the time step), and their interventions. Here the second sim has a lower β and a shorter step:

```{python}
S, I, R = ss.states('S I R')
infection = S >> I @ 1.5*I
recovery  = I >> R @ ss.days(8)
other = ss.Disease(infection, recovery, init_prev=0.001, name='measles')
other_sim = ss.Sim(other, total_pop=100_000, stop=ss.days(50), dt=ss.days(0.5), verbose=0)

ss.diff(sim, other_sim)
```

## Checking the numbers

A few numbers can be checked by hand. The run prints R0, which for an SIR is β × the infectious period; if it is far from what you expected, a rate or a duration is wrong, often in its units (see [Common pitfalls](troubleshooting_pitfalls.qmd#rates-durations-and-units)). In a closed population, the share of people ever infected depends only on R0 (it is about 80% for R0 = 2, and all but a few for measles), and the peak comes later the fewer people start infected.

Another check is to run the same model in another way. The ODE is the average course of the epidemic; run as agents, the model should follow it closely when there are many people, and differ by chance when there are few. A large difference that doesn't shrink with more people points to the size of the time step, or to something in the model that only one of them does. Here the same model is run both ways, as the scenarios of `ss.parallel()`:

```{python}
ode = ss.Sim(measles, total_pop=100_000, stop=ss.days(50), verbose=0)
agents = ss.Sim(measles, total_pop=100_000, n_agents=20_000, stop=ss.days(50), verbose=0)
msim = ss.parallel({'ODE': ode, 'Agents': agents})
msim.plot()
```

With `total_pop=100_000` and `n_agents=20_000`, each agent stands for five people, so the results of the two are on the same scale. The two reach about the same peak, but the agents reach it a few days later. With 20,000 agents and 20 infected at the start, that is not chance; the next section shows that it is the time step. [Solvers and when they disagree](running_solvers.qmd) says when to expect the solvers to differ, and why.

## Checking the time step

Agents, and stochastic compartmental models, take whole time steps: each step, people move between states with a probability worked out from the rates over that step. When the rates are high compared with the step (for measles, β = 1.9 per day against a step of 1 day), a smaller step can change the answer. `sim.check_dt()` runs the model with the step it has and with a step half as long, and shows how much each result changes:

```{python}
agent_sim = ss.Sim(measles, n_agents=20_000, stop=ss.days(50), verbose=0)
agent_sim.check_dt()
```

Each line is the largest difference between the two runs at any time, as a share of the result's largest value. The height of the peak of infectious people hardly changes, but the epidemic runs faster with the shorter step, so on a given day the counts differ by much more. The reason is that someone infected during a step can only infect others from the next step on: with R0 = 15 and an infectious period of 8 days, measles doubles in well under a day at first, so steps of a day hold it back. If the timing of the peak matters, use the smaller step (`dt=ss.days(0.5)`), and check again. For a stochastic run, part of each change is the difference between two runs, so a change of a few percent can be chance. (An ODE adjusts its own steps within each time step, so its results hardly depend on `dt`.)

## Finding what changes a parameter

Interventions and connectors change parameters while the model runs. When a parameter doesn't seem to have the value you expect, `sim.what_modifies()` lists everything that changes it:

```{python}
masks = ss.modify(measles.pars.beta, multiply=0.6, start=ss.days(10))
masked = ss.Sim(measles, total_pop=100_000, stop=ss.days(50), interventions=masks, verbose=0)
masked.what_modifies(measles.pars.beta)
```

## Looking inside a run

A model run as agents, or one with modules written as code, is run one step at a time, and within each step the modules are run in a fixed order: the loop. `sim.loop.to_df()` lists every call in it, in order, for the whole run; the first rows are the start and the first step:

```{python}
agent_sim.run()
agent_sim.loop.to_df().head(13)
```

::: {.callout-warning}
## [PROPOSAL]
The `time` column of `sim.loop.to_df()` shows each time as a duration in a mix of spellings (`days(0)`, `day`, `days(2)`). It should show plain numbers in the sim's unit (or dates, in a sim with dates), as the results do (P10, P14).
:::

To see what happens during a run, a function of the sim can be inserted into the loop, after (or, with `before=True`, before) any call in it. Here it prints the number infectious every ten days, just after the disease has taken its step:

```{python}
def show_infectious(sim):
    if sim.ti % 10 == 0:
        print('Day', sim.ti, 'infectious:', sim.diseases.measles.I.sum())

probed = ss.Sim(measles, n_agents=20_000, stop=ss.days(50), verbose=0)
probed.init()
probed.loop.insert(show_infectious, label='measles.step')
probed.run()
```

For anything more than a quick look, use an [analyzer](running_analyzers.qmd), which runs at the end of each step and can keep results of its own. Breakpoints and print statements in a module written as code work as in any Python program. A compartmental model that Starsim runs whole (an ODE with nothing that needs to happen between steps) has no loop to look into; inserting a function or adding an analyzer makes it run one step at a time, with the same results, and the run says so.

## Profiling

Compartmental models run in well under a second, so profiling is mostly for models run as agents, especially with networks or modules written as code. Start with how long each part of each step takes: run with `profile=True`, and plot the time spent in each call of the loop:

```{python}
big = ss.Sim(measles, n_agents=50_000, networks=ss.RandomNet(n_contacts=10), stop=ss.days(50), verbose=0)
big.run(profile=True)
big.loop.plot_cpu()
```

Here the network (`randomnet.step`, which pairs people up afresh each day) takes a large share of the time, as much as the disease. To see which lines of a function take the time, follow it with `sim.profile()`, which runs a copy of the sim with a line-by-line profiler on the functions given:

```{python}
big = ss.Sim(measles, n_agents=50_000, networks=ss.RandomNet(n_contacts=10), stop=ss.days(50), verbose=0)
prof = big.profile(follow=ss.RandomNet.add_pairs, plot=False)
```

The same works for a method of a module you wrote, which is where the time usually goes in a slow model: a loop over people in Python, where an operation on the whole array would do. `sim.cprofile()` profiles every function the run calls, which is useful when you don't yet know where to look. Only functions called during the run can be followed this way; for anything else, such as the building of the sim, use `sc.profile()` from Sciris directly.
